passages.t: An alliance with Ahab, and four hundred prophets
passages.happening:
‘Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honor in abundance, and he allied himself with Ahab by marriage’ (verse 1). Visiting Ahab in Samaria, he is asked to march against Ramoth-gilead, and answers, “I am like you, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war” (verse 3). But he adds, “Please inquire first for the word of the LORD” (verse 4).

Ahab gathers four hundred prophets, and they tell him to go up, ‘and God will deliver it into the hand of the king’ (verse 5). Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?” (verse 6). Ahab answers, “There is still one man who can ask the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad. He is Micaiah son of Imlah” (verse 7). While they wait, the prophets go on prophesying, and Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes iron horns to show how Ahab will gore the Arameans (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 17 showed Jehoshaphat at the height of his faithfulness. This chapter opens with the word that will shadow his reign and the next three: he joined himself to Ahab by marriage. Ahab, with his wife Jezebel, had promoted the worship of Baal. The marriage joined Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram to Ahab's daughter Athaliah, and it would bring Ahab's house and its idolatry into Jerusalem.

The chapter is nearly identical to 1 Kings 22, but in Chronicles it becomes the story of a good king of Judah who nearly dies because of a bad partnership. Ahab reigned about 874 to 853 BC. An inscription of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III, the Kurkh Monolith, names Ahab of Israel among the kings who faced Assyria at the Battle of Qarqar in 853 BC with a large force of chariots; his death at Ramoth-gilead is usually placed later that year. Ramoth-gilead was a fortified town east of the Jordan, fought over by Israel and the Arameans of Damascus.

Kings consulted prophets before war, and a king could keep a large company of court prophets. Ahab's four hundred are not called prophets of Baal; they speak in the LORD's name, but they tell the king what he wants to hear. Jehoshaphat distrusts their unanimous approval. Zedekiah's iron horns are a prophetic sign act, a dramatic gesture that pictured the message; horns stood for strength.
passages.later: Jeremiah later warned, “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes” (Jeremiah 23:16).
passages.asks: Ahab hated the one prophet who would not flatter him. Ask whose voice you avoid because it never tells you what you want to hear. And ask whether you have joined yourself to anyone in a way that will pull you where you should not go.

passages.happening:
The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the others. Micaiah answers, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever my God tells me” (verse 13). At first he echoes the four hundred, and Ahab demands the truth. Then: “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd” (verse 16).

He goes on: “I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing on His right and on His left” (verse 18). The LORD asks who will entice Ahab to fall at Ramoth-gilead, and a spirit offers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets (verses 19-21). ‘So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you’ (verse 22). Zedekiah strikes Micaiah in the face, and Ahab orders him to prison on bread and water until he returns safely (verses 23-26). Micaiah answers, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The chapter's central tension is four hundred voices against one. Every prophet says go up and prosper, and Micaiah alone will say only what the LORD tells him. His first answer repeats the others so exactly that Ahab hears it as sarcasm. His second gives two visions: the scattered sheep, and the heavenly council. Sheep without a shepherd drew on the old picture of a king as his people's shepherd; a scattered flock meant a dead king.

The verb entice, patah, can mean to persuade someone who is willing to be persuaded. Spirit, ruach, also means wind or breath. Ahab demands the truth, emet, from the prophet he has already said he hates for telling it.
passages.later: First Kings tells the same scene, and Ahab's same words: ‘There is still one man who can ask the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad’ (1 Kings 22:8).
passages.hard:
How can God send a lying spirit to deceive Ahab's prophets?

Interpreters read Micaiah's vision in several ways. Some take it as a real glimpse of the heavenly council, in which God permits a spirit to deceive Ahab as judgment on a king who had again and again chosen lies over truth. On this view God uses evil without being its author, much as in Job 1 and 2, or Paul's words about God sending a strong delusion on those who refused the truth. Others read it as a vision whose form fits the prophetic imagination of its time, meant to show that Ahab's prophets were deceived and that the deception was under God's judgment, not to describe the workings of heaven.

Many note that the vision is itself a warning. Micaiah tells Ahab exactly what is happening, so Ahab is not left without the truth. He hears it plainly and chooses the lie. The chapter does not answer every question about how God relates to evil, but it does show that God tells Ahab the truth and that Ahab is responsible for refusing it.
passages.asks: Micaiah was struck and imprisoned for telling the truth. Ask what it would cost you to say only what God says, when four hundred voices say otherwise. And ask whether you have ever struck back at someone for telling you a truth you did not want.

passages.t: A disguise, a random arrow, and a cry for help
passages.happening:
Ahab disguises himself and tells Jehoshaphat to wear his royal robes (verse 29). The king of Aram orders his chariot commanders to fight only the king of Israel (verse 30). Seeing Jehoshaphat, they turn on him, ‘but Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him’ (verse 31).

‘However, a certain man drew his bow without taking special aim, and he struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor’ (verse 33). Ahab props himself up in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening, ‘And at sunset he died’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The story fulfills the prophecy through a disguise that fails and an arrow shot at random, showing that no human plan escapes the word of the LORD. The irony is sharp: Ahab disguises himself to avoid death and dies, while Jehoshaphat, dressed as the target, lives. A king in royal robes was a visible target, which explains Ahab's disguise.

Chronicles follows 1 Kings 22 closely, with two changes. It leaves out the dogs licking Ahab's blood, which belongs to Elijah's word against Ahab in Kings, and it adds that when Jehoshaphat cried out, the LORD helped him, azar, the same verb that framed Asa's prayer. Even a king in the wrong alliance, in the wrong battle, could cry out and be heard.
passages.later: First Kings tells the same arrow: ‘However, a certain man drew his bow without taking special aim, and he struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor’ (1 Kings 22:34).
passages.asks: Jehoshaphat was in the wrong place, in another king's robes, and he cried out and was helped. Ask whether you believe God will hear you when you are where you should not be. And ask what disguise you have put on to avoid a word God has spoken.
